extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent attorneys, judges, and legal scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and doctrines governing when and how a patent may be amended by re-issue (what changes are permitted or forbidden, treatment of new matter, combination/sub-combination rules, and limits on broadening or narrowing claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may modify original claims
rubrics_metrics.description: That a re-issue may modify the Claims of the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities: Smith v. Merriam (1881), Woodward v. Dinsmore (1870), and Woodward v. Portland Co. (1880). The re-issue can both enlarge or restrict claims as necessary to cover the actual invention (e.g., Dorsey Harvester Rake Co. v. Marsh (1878)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may explain and claim forms described but not originally claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue may explain and claim a form of the invention described but not claimed in the original, when its importance has become apparent since the original was granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: Atwood v. Portland Co. (1880), American Nicholson Payment Co. v. Elizabeth (1873). Allows claiming forms that were described (but unclaimed) if their importance later appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may claim elements described but not claimed in original
rubrics_metrics.description: An element described but not claimed in the original patent may be claimed in the re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Loring v. Hall (1879), 15 O. G. 471.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may contain new claims founded on original description
rubrics_metrics.description: The re-issue may contain new Claims founded on the original Description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Combined Patents Can Co. v. Lloyd (1882), Union Paper Bag Co. v. Nixon (1873). New claim language may be used provided it is supported by the original disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may include new drawings based on original specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The re-issue may contain new drawings based on the original specification; the drawings of the re-issue may contain features not shown in the drawings of the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Union Paper Bag Co. v. Nixon (1873) and other cited cases. Drawings may be amended in matters outside the model if they do not affect claims (Pearl v. Appleton Co. (1880)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Matter once described as essential cannot be omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Matter once described in the original specification as essential to the invention cannot be omitted in the re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omission of matter treated as essential in the original is forbidden (see Russell v. Dodge (1876) and related authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Matter once disclaimed cannot be reclaimed (except narrow equity exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Matter once disclaimed — whether during Patent Office proceedings, in the original patent, or by subsequent disclaimer — cannot be reclaimed in a re-issue except where equity prevents estoppel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reclaiming disclaimed matter would enlarge the patented invention; only in limited cases where the applicant could not be regarded as estopped will reclamation be allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: New matter cannot be introduced into re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither directly nor indirectly can new matter be introduced into the re-issued patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated theme across cases: new matter is forbidden by statute and judicial decisions (see numerous citations including Russell v. Dodge and Stevens v. Pritchard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Immaterial elements may be dropped in re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: An immaterial element may be dropped in the re-issue if its omission does not affect the essence of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: McWilliams Mfg. Co. v. Blundell (1882), Union Paper Collar Co. v. Van Deusen (1872).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue can correct errors/defects to render patent operative but cannot interpolate new features
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents may be corrected to cure defects and supply deficiencies to render the patent operative and valid; but the patentee may not interpolate new features not described or substantially indicated in the specification, drawings, or Patent Office model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomas v. Shoe Machinery Mfg. Co. (1878) (Clifford, J.): corrections permitted to cure defects, but material interpolations exceed jurisdiction and render patent void (see 8 Bann. & A. 557 (560)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may be narrower than original if invention unchanged
rubrics_metrics.description: The re-issue may be narrower than the original if the invention is unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Gould v. Ballard (1878) and related cases: narrowing to conform to actual invention is allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlarged claims are carefully scrutinized for new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Enlarging claims in a re-issue is permissible only if no new matter is introduced; enlarged claims are to be carefully scrutinized to ensure they contain no new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: Tyler v. Welch (1880), Jenkins v. Stetson (1887). Courts examine whether enlargement introduces matter beyond original disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: New features allowed only if substantially suggested or indicated in original
rubrics_metrics.description: New features may not be introduced for the reason that every interpolation of the kind is forbidden, but the patentee may add whatever was substantially suggested or indicated in the original specifications, drawings, or Patent Office model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted from Stevens v. Pritchard (1876): errors/defects may be corrected, but new features not substantially suggested are forbidden. (10 O. G. 506; 2 Bann. & A. 890).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'new matter' (what counts as new matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: New matter is anything not embraced in the original specifications, drawings, and model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Dederick v. Cassell (1881) and related authorities. Also judicial formulations: new matter includes any change 'whereby a new and substantially different composition and results are secured.'

rubrics_metrics.name: New matter cannot be inserted even if later invented by patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: New matter cannot be inserted in the re-issue though invented by the patentee and inadvertently omitted from the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Atwater Mfg. Co. v. Beecher Mfg. Co. (1881); courts have rejected attempts to add later inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue standards stricter than application amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule as to the insertion of new matter is more strict in re-issues than in amendments to applications — the former governed by law, the latter by the discretion of the Commissioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Ex parte Bragg (1875) and related authorities: re-issue subject to legal prohibition; application amendments are discretionary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blanket prohibition on blending old and new matter in same claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue blending old matter and new matter in the same claim is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: Cahart v. Austin (1865) and 2 Clifford 528. Combination of new and old in same claim will invalidate the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: When original had no model/drawing, cannot insert new matter by asserting inventor had it in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the original patent had no model or drawing, no new matter can be inserted in the re-issue on the ground that the inventor had it in his mind when the original application was filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte Dieckerhoff (1877), 12 O. G. 429.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issued patent may embrace inventions defectively or insufficiently described in original (subject to joinder rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The re-issued patent may embrace all inventions which the original patent defectively or insufficiently described and claimed, subject to the rules governing the joinder of inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section §669: if the original described dependent or auxiliary inventions substantially indicated, the patentee may insert them in the re-issue unless abandoned or disclaimed; see Lockwood v. Morey and related discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee may insert dependent/auxiliary inventions that were substantially indicated
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the original specification described subordinate parts or additional inventions dependent on the principal one, and they were substantially indicated, the patentee (absent abandonment/estoppel) is permitted to insert such inventions in the re-issue if they could lawfully have been claimed in the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See §669 discussion and cited cases; the test is whether the inventor attempted to protect those dependent inventions as indicated in the original disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issued combination patent cannot embrace a combination essentially distinct from original
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issued combination-patent cannot embrace a combination essentially distinct from that described and claimed in the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §670: identity of combination rests on identity of elements and the cooperative law under which they operate; adding new elements or substituting non-equivalents makes the re-issue invalid (see Washburn & Moen v. Fuchs and other cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity test for combinations: elements and cooperative law
rubrics_metrics.description: The identity of the combination claimed in the re-issue with that described in the original depends upon the identity of their respective elements and of the cooperative law under which they are associated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the re-issue contains less than all elements described or substitutes a non-equivalent, it departs from the original combination and is void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot omit an essential element of an original combination
rubrics_metrics.description: The re-issue of a combination-patent is void if it omits one of the essential elements of the original invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Jenkins v. Stetson (1887), Neacy v. Allis (1882), Gammyer v. Newton (1879). Omitting an essential element is treated as a departure from the original invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot substitute a different element unless it is a mere equivalent (equivalence must be pointed out)
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue cannot substitute another element for one contained in the original unless the substituted element is a mere equivalent, and equivalence should be duly pointed out in the re-issue specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Blackman v. Kibbler (1879), Gill v. Wells (1874), National Spring Co. v. Union Car Spring Mfg. Co. (1874). Equivalents may be introduced but must be indicated and treated carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination patents may sometimes be re-issued to cover sub-combinations or elements, but boundaries must be strictly preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: When a principal combination is composed of sub-combinations, the re-issue may in some cases be extended to protect sub-combinations and elements entering into each sub-combination, but the dividing line between sub-combinations must be strictly preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A combination formed by adding a simple element to a complete sub-combination yields a principal combination and that sub-combination; only these subjects may be within the re-issue (see discussion in §670).

rubrics_metrics.name: A combination of simple elements contains no sub-combination; re-issue cannot cover fewer elements absent original description of such grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination composed solely of simple elements (each cooperating with every other) contains no sub-combination; a patent for such a combination cannot be re-issued to cover a less number of elements unless the original described the lesser grouping as forming a new material function or grouped them under a different cooperative method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Gill v. Wells (1874) and related discussion: where no suggestion exists that other inventions were intended, re-issue cannot reach sub-combinations that are truly new groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue is void if it departs from original combination's identity even if re-issued near expiration
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue is void when the original was for a combination only, if it covers a lesser combination of some of the original elements and is issued within four months of expiration of the original (and similarly where the re-issue departs from the original combination's identity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Gage v. Herring (1882) and related authorities; timing and substantial departure are relevant in evaluating validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of ambiguous words in re-issue does not enlarge scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The omission of ambiguous words in the re-issue does not enlarge it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Atlantic Giant Powder Co. v. Goodyear (1877) and other cases: mere deletion of ambiguous language will not be treated as expansion of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor's opinion in re-issue is permissible if it does not affect claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinion of the inventor, stated in the re-issue, as to the character of his invention is not improper if it does not affect the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Beed v. Chase (1885) and related cases: subjective statements are allowed so long as they don't alter claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue seeking to cover an infringing device will be closely scrutinized but valid if for same invention as original
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the re-issue seeks to cover an infringing device it will be closely scrutinized, but will be valid if clearly for the same invention as the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crompton v. Knowles (1881) and related authorities: courts examine whether the re-issue truly corresponds to original invention or introduces new matter to catch infringers.

rubrics_metrics.name: If re-issue does not clearly contain new matter substantially different, courts will hold it valid
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless it clearly appears that the re-issue contains new matters substantially different from the original, it will be held valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomas v. Shoe Machinery Mfg. Co. (1878) and related cases: presumption toward validity unless clear new matter exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where inventions are mutually inseparable, a patent for one covers the other
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the inventions are mutually inseparable, a patent for one independently covers the other and is a bar to any subsequent patent therefor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §669 discussion: inseparability implies the unclaimed invention was within intended scope or not abandoned; re-issue implications depend on whether inventions were separable or inseparable.
